# Pakistani Banknote Reader

> A free web app for blind and low-vision people in Pakistan: point a phone camera at a banknote and it says the value out loud in Urdu or English. It runs in the browser, works offline after the first visit, and uploads nothing. Deep Learning semester project by Hassan Ali Mehdi, Superior University, Lahore, under Dr. Munir Ahmad.

Full text for AI engines: https://boltanote.vercel.app/llms-full.txt

## Model
- Deployed: MobileNetV3-Large; input [1, 3, 224, 224] float32 RGB in [0,1] (whole photo squeezed to 224x224); output probs [1,15] over 10_front, 10_back, 20_front, 20_back, 50_front, 50_back, 100_front, 100_back, 500_front, 500_back, 1000_front, 1000_back, 5000_front, 5000_back, none. Add front+back per value.
- Weights: weights/boltanote.onnx (ONNX), weights/boltanote_torchscript.pt (TorchScript), weights/mobilenetv3_large.pt (PyTorch state_dict).
- Speaks if top value != none and probability >= 0.68.

## Results
- Internal test (727 photos): value accuracy 100.0%, wrong value said 0.0%.
- External test (63 photos, other photographers): 92.1%; 0 wrong amounts spoken, silent on 8.

## How to test
git clone https://github.com/Hassan-Ali-Mehdi-3024/boltanote && cd boltanote && pip install -r requirements.txt
python evaluate.py                          # 16 bundled labelled photos
python predict.py samples/500_front_1.jpg

## Questions and answers

### What is the Pakistani Banknote Reader?
A free web app for blind and low-vision people in Pakistan. You point a phone camera at a banknote and it says the value out loud in Urdu or English. It runs in the browser, so there is no app to install.

### How do I use it?
Open https://boltanote.vercel.app in a phone browser, tap Start camera, and hold a note in front of the camera. It says the value as soon as it is sure. With no camera, you can upload a photo or tap a test photo.

### Which Pakistani notes can it read?
All seven notes in circulation: Rs 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, 1,000 and 5,000, front or back, including folded or upside down. It knows the 2005–2008 designs, not the State Bank's new series.

### Is it free, and does it need an account?
It is free, with no account and no install. The code is open source under the MIT licence.

### Does it work offline?
Yes, after the first visit. The model, the runtime and the voice clips are saved on the phone, so it keeps working and reopens with no internet.

### Are my camera pictures uploaded anywhere?
No. Every picture is processed on the phone, inside the browser. Nothing is sent to a server.

### How accurate is it?
It names the value correctly on 100.0% of 727 unseen photos from the same dataset, and 92.1% of 63 photos taken by other people. On those 63 photos it spoke no wrong amount and stayed silent on 8. The first number mostly shows how alike the dataset's photos are; the second is closer to real use, but 63 photos is a small test.

### When does it stay silent?
It speaks only when it is at least 68% sure and three frames in a row agree, because saying a wrong amount is worse than saying nothing. The 0.68 threshold keeps wrong answers to at most 1 in 500 on a stress test of 2,940 hard, augmented validation photos.

### Does it work with screen readers?
It is built for them: results are announced to TalkBack and VoiceOver through a live region, every control is a large button, and on Android it also vibrates a code for each note. It has not yet been tested with blind users; that is the next step.

### Can it detect counterfeit notes?
No. It reads the value of a note and does not check whether the note is genuine. It also reads only one note at a time.

### Which model does it use?
MobileNetV3-Large, pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned to 15 classes: seven notes, front and back, plus "no note". It runs with ONNX Runtime Web and takes about 15 ms per photo on a CPU. It was compared with a CNN trained from scratch and MobileNetV4.

### What data was it trained on?
The Pakistan Image Currency Dataset (CC0) of 3,611 phone photos, plus 1,000 Imagenette photos for the "no note" class. A hash check found 339 of 402 photos in a second public dataset were near-copies of the first, so only the 63 new ones were used as the external test.

### Who made it?
Hassan Ali Mehdi, as a Deep Learning semester project at Superior University, Lahore (BSCS-7A), under Dr. Munir Ahmad, November 2026.

### Where are the code, weights and report?
The code, weights and data splits are at https://github.com/Hassan-Ali-Mehdi-3024/boltanote, and the report is at https://boltanote.vercel.app/report.pdf. Every link, with its alternate, is in the links section of this page.

### Is there a LinkedIn post?
No. Due to legal commitments with the company where I work, I can't use my LinkedIn for personal use while I'm employed there.

## Film transcript

Assalam o alaikum. I'm Hassan Ali Mehdi and this is a Pakistani banknote reader for blind people. You point your phone at a note and it tells you the value out loud in Urdu.

Pakistan has about 1.1 million blind people and most daily payments are still made in cash. Our seven notes differ only a little in size so a blind person usually has to ask a stranger which note is which, and trust the answer. Mixing up a 500 and a 5000 costs 4,500 rupees.

The reader is just a webpage. It reads the camera 4 times a second and speaks the value in Urdu or English with a recorded voice. So it works even on phones that have no Urdu speech. It stays silent when it is unsure because saying a wrong amount is worse than saying nothing. Once loaded, it works offline, it also vibrates a code and it works with screen readers.

I trained on a public dataset of 3,600 real phone photos, 7 notes front and back, many folded or half visible. I added a no note class with more than 1000 everyday photos so the model learns when to stay quiet.

Before trusting any number I checked whether the test photos were really new. I hashed every photo and found that 339 of the 402 test photos in a second public currency dataset are near copies of the first one. Only 63 were genuinely new. Without this check my external test would have looked perfect and meant nothing.

Training images are changed on the GPU every time they are seen: any angle, too close, half out of frame, fingers over the note, dim or yellow light, and blur. No mirror flips because the camera never sees a mirrored note.

I compared a CNN trained from scratch with two phone networks pretrained on ImageNet: MobileNet version 3, and the new MobileNet version 4. On photos from the same dataset, all three are almost perfect. On photos taken by other people the difference shows: transfer learning holds up far better. I deployed MobileNet version 3 Large, the best on validation and also the fastest.

Here are the honest numbers. 100% on unseen photos from the same dataset but 92% on photos by other people. And on those photos, it never said a wrong amount. The first number mostly shows how alike the dataset photos are. The others are what a real user would get.

The most important design decision is when to speak. On ordinary validation photos, the model is almost never wrong. So any threshold looks safe. So I calibrated on a stress test: every validation photo four times. The app speaks only above 0.68 confidence and only when three frames in a row agree.

Here is a live demo. I open the site on my phone, tap start camera and hold a note in front of it. It reads several frames per second and speaks the value with nothing installed.

Its limits. The training photos only show a few physical notes, per value. It knows the current note design but not the State Bank's new series. It reads one note at a time and it does not detect counterfeits. Next, worn notes counting a whole handful and a test with blind users is what's coming next.

Everything is open. The website, the code, the weights, the data splits are all linked. Thank you for watching.

## Full report

← Pakistani Banknote Reader
A talking Pakistani banknote reader for blind people, tested beyond its own dataset
Hassan Ali Mehdi · BS Computer Science (7A), Superior University, Lahore · Deep Learning, instructor Dr. Munir Ahmad · November 2026
Live demo: https://boltanote.vercel.app · Code, weights & data splits: https://github.com/Hassan-Ali-Mehdi-3024/boltanote · Video: https://youtu.be/P0O-qhMldGI
Abstract. Blind people in Pakistan (about 1.1 million [1]) cannot tell banknotes apart without help, and a Rs 500 / Rs 5,000 mix-up costs Rs 4,500. The reader is a web app that reads the phone camera about four times a second and says the note's value aloud in Urdu (پانچ سو روپے) or English, offline once loaded. We fine-tune MobileNetV3-Large [2] and MobileNetV4-Conv-Medium [3] and train a CNN from scratch on a public dataset of 3,611 phone photos (15 classes: seven notes × front/back, plus "no note"). Before measuring anything we checked how much the public data repeats itself: 339 of the 402 test photos in a second public currency dataset are near-copies of the first, leaving 63 genuinely new photos. The deployed MobileNetV3-Large scores 100.0% on unseen photos from the training dataset but 92.1% on photos by other people. Because saying a wrong amount is worse than saying nothing, the app speaks only above a confidence threshold calibrated on a stress-tested validation set.
1. Problem
Cash is still how most everyday purchases in Pakistan are paid. The seven notes in circulation (Rs 10 to Rs 5,000) differ only modestly in size, so a blind person usually has to ask someone and trust the answer. Commercial apps exist for some currencies, but an assistant for Pakistani notes should work on cheap phones, speak Urdu, and need no installation. The cost of errors is asymmetric: silence just means "move the note and try again", while a wrong value can cost real money.
Contributions. (1) A working Urdu-speaking reader that runs in any phone browser. (2) A measurement of hidden duplication in public currency datasets, and an evaluation that goes beyond the training dataset: other photographers. (3) A speaking rule that trades coverage for safety, calibrated without touching test data. (4) An accuracy-versus-speed comparison of three architectures for phones.
2. Data
Training data. The Pakistan Image Currency Dataset [7] (CC0) has 3,611 phone photos of the 2005–2008 note series, each value front and back, many folded, partly visible, or in a hand, plus 280 "other" photos. We add 1,000 Imagenette photos [6] (100 per class) to the "no note" class so the model learns to stay silent.
Duplicate check. We computed a 64-bit perceptual hash [9] of every photo and joined photos within 8 bits of each other. Inside the training dataset, near-copies are kept on the same side of the 70 / 15 / 15 per-class split (seed 42). Against the Roboflow currency dataset [8], which we intended as an independent test, 339 of 402 single-note test photos turned out to be near-copies of training photos; only 63 remain as a genuine external test. Without this check that external test would have reported near-perfect accuracy.
SplitPhotos
Train | 3,429 |
Validation | 735 |
Same-dataset test | 727 |
External test (other photographers) | 63 |
3. Method
Each model sees the whole camera frame squeezed to 224 × 224 (the same preprocessing in training, predict.py and the browser) and outputs 15 class probabilities; front and back are separate classes because they look nothing alike, and the app adds them per value. Augmentation is designed around how blind users actually hold notes: any rotation, too close or too far, half the note out of frame, fingers over it, dim or yellow light, motion blur. Mirror flips are excluded because the camera never sees a mirrored note.
SettingValue
Input | RGB photo, whole frame squeezed to 224 × 224, values in [0, 1] (cached at 320 px for augmentation) |
Classes | 15 = 7 values × front/back + none |
Optimiser | AdamW, weight decay 0.05, label smoothing 0.1 |
Learning rate | 1e-3 (MobileNets), 2e-3 (scratch); 5% warm-up then cosine |
Epochs | 40 (MobileNets), 80 (scratch); best epoch by validation value accuracy |
Batch | 64, bfloat16 mixed precision, 1 × NVIDIA L4 (Colab) |
Augmentation (GPU) | rotation ±180°, zoom 0.85–1.9×, stretch 0.8–1.25, shift ±18%, 0–2 finger/shadow patches, brightness/contrast ±35%, gamma ±30%, saturation ±40%, colour cast ±8%, noise, blur (p = 0.3); no mirror flips |
Speaking threshold | lowest threshold with
When to speak. On ordinary validation photos the model is almost never wrong, so any threshold looks safe there (the lowest we searched, 0.40, already gives no more than 1 wrong answer in 500). Modern networks are over-confident on data like their training data [10]. We therefore calibrate on a stress validation set: each validation photo four times with the training augmentations. Because a wrong amount costs real money, we require at most 1 wrong value in 500 there (0.2%); the lowest threshold that achieves it is 0.68. The app additionally requires the same answer in three consecutive frames before speaking.
4. Results
ModelParamsONNXCPU msSame-dataset testOther photographersThreshold
CNN from scratch | 2.36M | 9.4 MB | 88 | 99.6% | 82.5% | 0.76 |
MobileNetV3-Large (deployed) | 4.22M | 16.9 MB | 15 | 100.0% | 92.1% | 0.68 |
MobileNetV4-Conv-Medium | 8.45M | 33.7 MB | 37 | 99.9% | 92.1% | 0.70 |
All models are near-perfect on unseen photos from the training dataset, which mostly shows how similar those photos are to each other. The informative columns are the other two: on photos by other people the deployed model drops by 7.9 points, and the scratch CNN, which matched the pretrained models on the same-dataset test, falls to 82.5%. ImageNet pretraining buys robustness that the in-dataset test cannot show. MobileNetV3-Large runs in 15 ms per photo on a 2-core CPU, MobileNetV4-Conv-Medium in 37 ms (2.5× slower, 2.0× the parameters).

Figure 4. Training loss and validation accuracy.
5. Deployment
The deployed model is exported to ONNX (opset 17, 16.9 MB, softmax included) and TorchScript. The website runs it with ONNX Runtime Web on the phone, on the live rear camera, about four frames a second; the speech is pre-recorded with neural Urdu and English voices so it works even on phones without Urdu text-to-speech, and Android phones also vibrate a code (1–4 short pulses for Rs 10–100, 1–3 long for Rs 500–5,000). Results are announced in an ARIA live region so screen readers (TalkBack, VoiceOver) read them too. The repository holds code, splits, all weights with SHA-256 hashes in model_card.json, the executed notebook, and a GitHub Actions test.
6. Limitations
The training photos show a few physical notes per value on similar indoor backgrounds; very worn, torn or taped notes are under-represented.
It knows the 2005–2008 designs; the State Bank of Pakistan's announced new series will need new photos and retraining.
One note at a time; it is not a counterfeit detector.
The external test has only 63 photos, so its uncertainty is large (one photo ≈ 1.6 points).
7. Conclusion
A phone-sized network reads Pakistani banknotes aloud in Urdu, offline, in any browser. The headline in-dataset accuracy is close to perfect, but the honest numbers come from photos the dataset never saw, and a speaking rule tuned for safety matters as much as raw accuracy. Next: photos of worn notes, the new note series, counting several notes in one frame, and a field test with blind users.
